items.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024
items.q: ooh, night and day. You know? Rich Redman, the country drummer? Night and day. But they’ve all got the same skills and they all applied them in their own way. Not my way, their way.

ctx.x: Oh jeez. I can’t answer that. I don’t know. I’ll tell you why I can’t answer it. It’s because everybody’s different. And my philosophy became, when I first started out and how I related to a student is I was dead set on making this person the greatest drummer in the world, and which I realized later on was just a huge ego trip on my part, so that I could say I created that drummer. And I realized that not everybody is meant to be the greatest drummer in the world — whatever that means — but I realized that my job…

my teaching is none of my students play like me. I mean that’s the greatest compliment ever that a teacher can be given. And they’re all distinct personalities. Everybody — take Ari Hoenig and Keith Carlock — ooh, night and day. You know? Rich Redman, the country drummer? Night and day. But they’ve all got the same skills and they all applied them in their own way. Not my way, their way. It’s just like you teach somebody language. They learn how to use it their way. That’s the same thing you do with music, with…
What a path you’ve had. Would you have ever, under the guise of making a living, taught students or addressed students about programming drum machines?
